items.item: spark.default.parallelism's local-mode definition (core count) is a special case of its general rule: for parent-RDD operations like reduceByKey/join it's the largest number of partitions already present in a parent RDD, not a cluster-wide constant.

at.step: Reveal: default parallelism is the core count

items.item: spark.sql.shuffle.partitions applies only to DataFrame/SQL-layer shuffles (joins, aggregations); it has no effect on a plain RDD's parallelize or map, which is exactly why the two settings this topic measures never interact.

AQE's coalescePartitions feature (on by default in Spark 4.x) can shrink a shuffle's actual runtime partition count below spark.sql.shuffle.partitions for small data — this topic's own examples.py disables AQE specifically to measure the configured setting cleanly, disclosed as a methodology note rather than silently hidden.

at.out: AQE and coalescePartitions is this chapter's own later topic to measure directly; named only as a methodology disclosure here

items.item: The four locality levels (PROCESS_LOCAL, NODE_LOCAL, RACK_LOCAL, ANY) form a strict preference order the scheduler tries from best to worst, waiting spark.locality.wait milliseconds at each level before dropping to the next — local mode's single JVM means PROCESS_LOCAL is always immediately available, so no drop and no wait is ever observable.

at.step: Reveal: locality has nowhere to go here

items.item: Dynamic allocation (spark.dynamicAllocation.enabled) scales executor count up and down with workload, but since Spark 3.0 it requires either an external shuffle service or shuffle tracking (spark.dynamicAllocation.shuffleTracking.enabled) so a shrinking executor's shuffle files aren't lost mid-job — named as a real production dependency, not measured, since local mode has exactly one executor and nothing to scale.

at.deep: Dynamic allocation and the shuffle-tracking requirement

items.item: FAIR scheduling's pools (configured via fairscheduler.xml) let independent jobs, not just tasks within one job, share a cluster's resources concurrently instead of queueing strictly behind each other — the production case this topic names is multiple users or applications sharing one long-running SparkContext (e.g. a notebook server), not a single batch job.

spark.default.parallelism and spark.sql.shuffle.partitions being independent also means raising core count alone (more executors) never changes an existing job's shuffle output partition count — a common production surprise when scaling a cluster up doesn't reduce small-file or small-partition overhead the way engineers expect.

at.out: named as a production consequence; not independently measured, since local mode can't vary executor count at all

items.item: The 'legacy' locality-wait-reset heuristic TaskSchedulerImpl.scala documents (resetting the wait timer on every task launch rather than only on a fair-share offer) was changed as of a specific SPARK JIRA because it let a popular TaskSet starve other locality levels indefinitely — named only as a historical note from the source's own comment, not independently sourced further.

at.out: historical implementation detail named only in passing from the quoted scaladoc; not a separate syllabus clause

items.item: Catalyst's AQE can also raise, not just lower, the number of reduce-side tasks actually scheduled relative to spark.sql.shuffle.partitions in the opposite direction (skew-join splitting), the mirror case to the coalescing this topic's methodology note disables — named only as a forward pointer to the chapter's later AQE/skew topics.

at.out: forward pointer only; AQE skew handling is this chapter's own later topic

items.item: Both parallelism settings are read, not just set, at different times in a job's life: spark.default.parallelism is consulted once, when an RDD with no parent is created, while spark.sql.shuffle.partitions is consulted fresh at each shuffle's own planning time — which is exactly why this topic's third measurement (changing the config, then checking both a new shuffle and a new bare RDD) can observe one move and the other not, in the same session.
